extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing USPTO examination guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate whether patent claims are directed to patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101 using the two-step Alice/Mayo framework and USPTO form-paragraph guidance. Includes procedures for statutory-category determination, judicial-exception analysis, markedly-different characteristics for nature-based products, and drafting rejection form paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory Category Determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1 determines whether the claim is directed to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is not directed to one of these statutory categories, reject the claim under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as being drawn to non-statutory subject matter, using revised form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01, and continue examination for patentability. This step has not changed and is explained in MPEP 2106(I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2 — Two-part Alice/Mayo Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2 is the two-part analysis from Alice Corp. (also called the Mayo test) for claims directed to laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas (the judicially recognized exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This two-part test is represented in diamonds (2A) and (2B) in the flowchart and is the subject of the Interim Eligibility Guidance. Use Step 2A to determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception and Step 2B to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — 'Directed to' a Judicial Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step 2A, determine whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea (judicial exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Directed to' means the exception is recited in the claim, i.e., the claim sets forth or describes the exception. If no, the claim is eligible and examination should continue for patentability. If yes, proceed to Step 2B. Examples of concepts courts have found to be laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas are provided in Parts I.A.2 and IV of the Interim Eligibility Guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis when claim does not 'tie up' exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim, when viewed as a whole, clearly does not seek to 'tie up' any judicial exception, use the streamlined analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'streamlined analysis' discussed in Part I.B.3 of the Interim Eligibility Guidance when it is clear that a claim does not attempt to preempt all practical applications of an exception. (See referenced part for application guidance and examples.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly Different Characteristics analysis for nature-based products
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim recites a nature-based product limitation, use the markedly different characteristics analysis to evaluate whether the claim is directed to a 'product of nature' that falls under the law of nature and natural phenomenon exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine whether the markedly different characteristics analysis is needed, and how to perform this analysis, see Part I.A.3 of the Interim Eligibility Guidance. For products of nature, explain how the characteristics are not markedly different from the product’s naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state when asserting an exception (example wording provided in form paragraph guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — 'Significantly More' / Inventive Concept Inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step 2B, determine whether any element, or combination of elements, in the claim is sufficient to ensure that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no, the claim is ineligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101 using form paragraphs 7.05 [revised] and 7.05.015 [new]. If yes, the claim is eligible. The additional elements should be considered both individually and as an ordered combination. Individual elements when viewed on their own may not appear to add significantly more, but when viewed in combination may amount to significantly more than the exception. The Supreme Court has identified a number of considerations for determining whether a claim with additional elements amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself; examples and applications are in Parts I.B.1 and III of the Interim Eligibility Guidance. Consider each claim separately based on the particular elements recited therein — claims do not automatically rise or fall with similar claims in an application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of claims directed to multiple exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a plurality of exceptions, conduct the eligibility analysis for one of the exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional elements that satisfy Step 2B for one exception will likely satisfy Step 2B for all exceptions in a claim. Conversely, if the claim fails under Step 2B for one exception, the claim is ineligible and no further eligibility analysis is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form Paragraph 7.05 — Rejection Heading (Procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 7.05 is the rejection header for 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner Note: (1) This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.04.01 in first actions and final rejections. (2) This form paragraph must be followed by a detailed explanation of the grounds of rejection using one or more of form paragraphs - 7.05.01, 7.05.015, 7.05.02, 7.05.03, or another appropriate reason. (3) See MPEP §§ 706.03(a) and 2105 - 2107.03 for additional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form Paragraph 7.05.01 — Non-Statutory (Not One of the Four Statutory Categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 7.05.01 when the claimed invention is directed to non-statutory subject matter because it does not fall within at least one of the four categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner Note: (1) This form paragraph should be preceded by form paragraph 7.05. (2) In bracket 1, explain why the claimed invention is not patent eligible subject matter by identifying what the claim(s) is/are directed to and explain why it does not fall within at least one of the four categories, e.g., the claim(s) is/are directed to a signal per se, mere information in the form of data, a contract between two parties, or a human being (see MPEP § 2106, subsection I). (3) For a claim that is directed to a judicial exception (i.e., a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea) and is non-statutory, use form paragraph 7.05.015.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form Paragraph 7.05.015 — Non-Statutory (Directed to Judicial Exception without Significantly More)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 7.05.015 is used when the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea) without significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text template: 'the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception (i.e., a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea) without significantly more. Claim(s) [1] is/are directed to [2]. The claim(s) does/do not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception because [3].' Examiner Note guidance: (1) This form paragraph should be preceded by form paragraph 7.05. (2) This form paragraph is for use with all claims, including product (machine, manufacture, and composition of matter) and process claims, and for any type of judicial exception. (3) In bracket 1, identify the claim or claims that recite the judicial exception. (4) In bracket 2, identify the exception by referring to how it is recited (set forth or described) in the claim and explain why it is considered an exception (examples: 'the Arrhenius equation, which is a law of nature in the form of a mathematical algorithm' or 'the series of steps instructing how to hedge risk, which is a fundamental economic practice and thus an abstract idea'). For products of nature, explain how the characteristics are not markedly different from the product’s naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state (example wording provided). (5) In bracket 3, identify the additional elements and explain why, when considered separately and in combination, they do not add significantly more to the exception (examples: generically recited computer elements do not add a meaningful limitation because they would be routine in any computer implementation; routine data-gathering steps do not add a meaningful limitation because they would be routinely used by those of ordinary skill in the art).
